title: The NoSQL families and when each wins

claims.text: The 2007 paper describes a highly available key-value storage system used by core services to provide an always-on experience, and is explicit about the trade: to achieve that level of availability it sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios, making extensive use of object versioning and application-assisted conflict resolution. It prioritises availability and performance over consistency while allowing application-specific control of the trade-offs.

source.title: Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, Madan Jampani, Gunavardhan Kakulapati, Avinash Lakshman, Alex Pilchin, Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, Peter Vosshall and Werner Vogels, Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, Proceedings of the 21st ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 2007, pages 205-220, doi 10.1145/1294261.1294281

claims.text: Its techniques are named as a synthesis of well-known ones rather than as inventions: data is partitioned and replicated using consistent hashing, consistency among replicas is facilitated by object versioning and maintained during updates by a quorum-like technique and a decentralised replica synchronisation protocol, and membership and failure detection use a gossip-based protocol. The system has no isolation and allows only single-key updates.

source.title: Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, Madan Jampani, Gunavardhan Kakulapati, Avinash Lakshman, Alex Pilchin, Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, Peter Vosshall and Werner Vogels, Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, Proceedings of the 21st ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 2007, pages 205-220, doi 10.1145/1294261.1294281

beats.broke: the relational guarantees are a package — a single consistent view, transactions across rows, joins at read time — and a system that must stay writeable during a partition cannot have all of them
beats.fix: unbundle the package and keep only what the workload needs, which produces families rather than one alternative: a key-value store, a document store, a wide-column store, a graph store, each dropping different guarantees for different gains
beats.cost: what is dropped is dropped for the whole system rather than per query, so a workload that later needs the discarded guarantee has to reimplement it in application code, usually worse
beats.interview: what the well-known alternative to the relational model actually gave up, and what it got
